sentences.text: This creature measured five meters across its wings and weighed roughly fifteen kilograms.
Its upper arm bone, or humerus, featured a muscle attachment ridge positioned unusually close to the body compared to other species.
The lower end of this bone expanded into a broad, triangular shape.
The forearm bone, known as the ulna, was relatively short and wide with a massively enlarged upper end.
The discovery of Tethydraco proves that pterosaur diversity during the final stage of the Cretaceous was far greater than scientists once believed.
Nicholas R. Longrich, David M. Martill, and Brian Andres formally named the species Tethydraco regalis in 2018.
The defining specimen, called the holotype, was found in late Maastrichtian phosphate layers in Morocco and consists of a single, crushed left upper arm bone.

Other fossils linked to the species include forearm bones, thigh bones, and a combined leg bone, though connecting these fragments to the main specimen remains difficult due to a lack of matching bone parts.
Tethydraco shared its environment in the Ouled Abdoun Basin with other flying reptiles like Phosphatodraco and Alcione, as well as the meat-eating dinosaur Chenanisaurus.
When first described, the animal was placed in the family Pteranodontidae.

Later studies in 2021 suggested it might be an azhdarchid or even the same animal as Phosphatodraco, while some researchers initially argued the arm shape pointed to azhdarchids before confirming it as a pteranodontid.
In 2023, new analysis noted that the wing shape of a specimen assigned to Tethydraco differs from the original bone, making its classification complicated.
Cladistic analysis identified Tethydraco as the closest relative to a group containing Pteranodon and Geosternbergia.
This animal lived approximately sixty-six million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Maastrichtian stage in what is now Morocco.

The existence of Tethydraco is considered evidence that pterosaur diversity was higher than previously thought, challenging the idea that these creatures went extinct earlier than the mass extinction event. Some researchers debate whether the apparent decline of pterosaurs is an illusion caused by the Signor–Lipps effect, where the most recent fossils are found in older layers than the actual extinction event.
